evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: During President Bill Clinton's first and second terms of office, he nominated 24 people for 20 federal appellate judgeships but the nominees were not processed by the Republican-controlled Senate Judiciary Committee.

evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: Three of the nominees who were not processed (Christine Arguello, Andre M. Davis and S. Elizabeth Gibson) were nominated after July 1, 2000, the traditional start date of the unofficial Thurmond Rule during a presidential election year.

evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: Democrats claim that Senate Republicans of the 106th Congress purposely tried to keep open particular judgeships as a political maneuver to allow a future Republican president to fill them.

evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: Of the 20 seats in question, four were eventually filled with different Clinton nominees, fourteen were later filled with Republican nominees by President George W. Bush and two continued to stay open during Bush's presidency.

evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: Senator Harry Reid, the Democratic leader of the United States Senate during the 110th Congress, and Senator Patrick Leahy, the Democratic leader of the Senate Judiciary Committee under Reid, repeatedly mentioned the controversy over President Clinton's court of appeals nominees during the controversy involving the confirmation of Republican court of appeals nominees during the last two years of Bush's second term.

evidence.title: Bill Clinton judicial appointment controversies
evidence.text: Republicans claimed that Democrats were refusing to confirm certain longstanding Bush nominees in order to allow a future Democratic president in 2009 to fill those judgeships.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: Lula Johnson Davis was Secretary for the Majority of the United States Senate from 2008 to 2011.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: Davis was born in Louisiana.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: She received a B.S. in office administration and an M.Ed., in guidance counseling from Southern University in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: She began her career with the Senate as a legislative correspondent for Senator Russell B. Long of Louisiana.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: After Senator Long retired from the Senate in January 1987, Davis worked as an office assistant for the Democratic Policy Committee’s Senate floor staff office.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: In 1993, she became a member of the Democratic floor staff.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: In 1995, she was promoted to chief floor assistant.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: In 1997, she assumed the position of assistant secretary.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: After the retirement of Martin P. Paone, in January 2008, the Senate elected Davis Secretary for the Majority.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: As Secretary for the Majority, she was a senior procedural advisor to the Senate Majority Leader, Senator Harry Reid, and supervised the day-to-day Senate schedule.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: In so doing, she often worked with Secretary for the Minority David J. Schiappa.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: Davis told Senators what they could and could not do when it came to rules and procedure.

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: Consequently, Davis was called “one of the most powerful unelected people in the U.S. Senate.”

evidence.title: Lula J. Davis
evidence.text: Davis retired at the end of the 111th Congress.

evidence.title: Bob Beers (Nevada)
evidence.text: Robert T. Beers (born October 14, 1959) is an American accountant (CPA) and member of the Republican Party who currently serves as a member of the Las Vegas City Council, representing Ward 2.

evidence.title: Bob Beers (Nevada)
evidence.text: He was previously a member of the Nevada Assembly from 1998 to 2004 and the Nevada Senate from 2005 to 2008.

evidence.title: Bob Beers (Nevada)
evidence.text: He ran unsuccessfully for the Republican nomination for Governor of Nevada in 2006 and in January 2014, he announced that he would run against Democratic Senator Harry Reid in the 2016 U.S. Senate election, but he withdrew from the race in June 2015.

evidence.title: Rory Reid
evidence.text: Rory Jason Reid (born July 11, 1963) is an American attorney and politician.

evidence.title: Rory Reid
evidence.text: He served as elected Chairman of the Clark County Commission in Clark County, Nevada and was the Democratic nominee for Governor of Nevada in the 2010 gubernatorial election.

evidence.title: Rory Reid
evidence.text: Reid is a member of the Democratic Party and a son of former United States Senator Harry Reid.

evidence.title: Rory Reid
evidence.text: In 2007, the "Las Vegas Sun" called Reid a political "rising star" in Nevada.
